incidents.title: Single-region blast radius
incidents.brief: An availability-zone storm takes the only region offline and the product is unreachable worldwide.
incidents.constraint: RTO is 15 minutes; RPO is near-zero for orders.
incidents.question: What architecture reduces that blast radius?

choices.label: Second region
choices.resultBody: Run a second region with failover (or active-active) rather than one regional stack.

choices.label: Bigger VM
choices.resultBody: A larger VM still lives inside US-East, the region that is down, so all 15,000 req/s keep failing until the whole region recovers.

choices.label: More disks
choices.resultBody: The extra disks attach in the same offline region; errors stay above 5,000 and the 15-minute RTO is blown while you wait for the provider.

hints: One region is the blast radius.
Failover must already have capacity.
Serve from a second region.

incidents.title: 40% of users stuck on a dead region after DNS flip
incidents.brief: us-east went dark and TicketHub switched its DNS record to us-west in 2 minutes. With a 3600 s TTL and pooled keep-alive connections, 40% of 60k req/s still hit us-east 45 minutes later.
incidents.constraint: You can't control client resolvers, ISP caches or how long apps keep connections open.
incidents.question: How do you move traffic without waiting on DNS caches?

choices.label: Static anycast IPs on a global load balancer with endpoint health checks

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Paid edge service; clients keep one IP forever and failover happens behind it.

choices.resultBody: Clients resolve two anycast IPs that never change; the edge health-checks each region and shifts traffic to us-west within about 30 s, regardless of what any resolver has cached. New connections land on us-west immediately. Cost: roughly $1.8k a month for the edge service plus data-transfer fees.

choices.label: Cut the DNS record's TTL from 3600 seconds to 5
choices.resultBody: Next time, many ISP resolvers floor TTLs at 60-300 s and mobile apps hold keep-alive connections for hours without re-resolving, so 12% of traffic still reaches the dead region; DNS query volume also rises 700x.

choices.label: Publish both regions' IPs in one multi-value A record
choices.resultTitle: Half the connects wait for timeouts
choices.resultBody: Clients pick an IP at random, and many SDKs don't try the second address until a 21 s TCP timeout; half of new connections stall on the dead region before failing or falling back.

hints: The DNS change was fast; getting clients to notice it was slow.
Any fix that relies on clients re-resolving inherits every cache between you and them.
Keep the IP the same and change what's behind it.

incidents.title: Failover drops 12 minutes of orders
incidents.brief: ShopNorth failed over from us-east to us-west. Async replication had silently fallen 12 minutes behind, so about 9,400 orders (13 orders/s) never reached the promoted replica.
incidents.constraint: Finance caps RPO at 5 seconds, and checkout p95 cannot absorb a 70 ms cross-region commit.
incidents.question: What keeps the next failover inside the 5-second RPO?

choices.label: Lag SLO: page at 2 s, throttle writes past 5 s
choices.resultTitle: Replication lag is now a budget
choices.resultBody: Lag is a paged metric: 2 s wakes on-call and 5 s applies write backpressure at checkout. Worst-case loss drops from 9,400 orders to about 65, at the price of occasional checkout throttling when the WAN link degrades.

choices.label: Synchronous cross-region commit on every order write
choices.resultBody: Nothing is lost now, but each commit waits a 70 ms round trip and checkout makes four writes; p95 climbs from 180 to 460 ms, far past the latency budget.

choices.label: Automate DNS failover so promotion takes under a minute
choices.resultBody: Promotion now takes 50 seconds instead of 20 minutes, which fixes RTO. The replica is still 12 minutes behind with nobody watching, so the next failover drops the same 9,400 orders.

hints: RTO and RPO are different numbers, and this outage broke the second one.
Async replication is acceptable only if you know how far behind it is.
Treat replica lag as a budget you measure, alert on, and enforce at write time.

incidents.title: Singapore customers served from Virginia
incidents.brief: Deskly added ap-southeast-1 and geo-DNS, yet enterprise users in Singapore still see 240 ms RTT: their corporate resolvers sit at HQ in Virginia, so DNS maps them to us-east. Page loads take 2.8 s.
incidents.constraint: Customers won't change their corporate DNS setup for one vendor.
incidents.question: How do you route by where the user is, not where their resolver is?

choices.label: Terminate TLS at the nearest edge and route by client IP

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Edge sees the real client address; adds an edge hop and per-GB fees.

choices.resultTitle: The edge sees the real user
choices.resultBody: Anycast delivers each TCP connection to the nearest point of presence, which sees the true client address and forwards to ap-southeast-1 over the provider backbone. The resolver's location no longer matters, and page loads fall to 0.7 s. Cost: edge fees and one more hop to operate.

choices.label: Add finer country rules to the geo-DNS map
choices.resultBody: The rules are correct but the input is wrong: every lookup still arrives from the Virginia resolver, and corporate resolvers rarely forward EDNS Client Subnet, so the map keeps choosing us-east.

choices.label: Cache API responses on the CDN in Singapore
choices.resultBody: Static assets speed up, but ticket lists and inboxes are per-user and uncacheable, so the hit rate on API calls is 3% and each page still makes five 240 ms round trips to Virginia.

hints: Geo-DNS decides based on who asks the DNS question.
For these users the asker is thousands of kilometres away from the user.
Make the routing decision at a point that sees the user's own connection.

incidents.title: One bad flag took down all three regions at once
incidents.brief: StreamCo pushed a rate-limit config with limit: 0 through its global config service. All three regions picked it up within 40 s and rejected 100% of 180k req/s. Multi-region bought nothing.
incidents.constraint: Config changes must still reach all regions within an hour.
incidents.question: How do you stop one change from hitting every region together?

choices.label: Roll config region by region with bake time and auto-rollback

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Global changes take ~45 min; regions run different config versions during the rollout.

choices.resultBody: The change goes to 5% of ap-south, then the whole region, then the next, with 15 minutes of bake between stages. The next bad value trips the error-rate alarm in the canary slice and rolls back automatically, so only a sliver of one region is affected. Cost: global changes take about 45 minutes.

choices.label: Add a fourth region for extra failover capacity
choices.resultBody: The new region subscribes to the same config service and receives the same bad value at the same moment, so the outage just has one more region in it and costs 33% more.

choices.label: Require two engineers to approve every config change
choices.resultBody: Review catches some mistakes, but the next bad value looks reasonable in a diff, both reviewers approve it, and it still lands on every region at once with the same 100% rejection.

hints: The regions were independent for hardware failures, not for changes.
Most large outages start with a deploy or a config push.
Make regions separate failure domains for changes too, and give each stage time to show errors.

incidents.title: Failover logs out two million users
incidents.brief: BankLite failed over from us-east to us-west during a drill. Sessions live only in us-east Redis, so all 2.1M active users were logged out and 380k called support or retried MFA at once.
incidents.constraint: A revoked session must stop working in every region within 5 seconds.
incidents.question: How does a session survive a region failover?

choices.label: Replicate the session store asynchronously into each region

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Second Redis cluster; revocations and new sessions reach other regions in ~1 s.

choices.resultBody: Each region reads a local Redis that receives every session write and revocation about a second later. On failover, us-west already holds nearly all sessions; only sessions created in the last second are lost. Revocations propagate well inside the 5 s budget. Cost: a second cluster and cross-region replication traffic.

choices.label: Pin each user's traffic to their home region
choices.resultTitle: Pinned to the region that died
choices.resultBody: Stickiness keeps users near their session in normal times, but when the home region is the one that fails, every pinned user still loses their session and the login storm is identical.

choices.label: Have us-west pods read sessions from us-east over WAN
choices.resultTitle: Session store died with its region
choices.resultBody: In normal times every request pays a 70 ms cross-region lookup, and when us-east is actually down the store is unreachable too, so all 2.1M users are logged out anyway.

hints: The standby had compute but not the state users depend on.
Anything stored only in the failed region is gone during the failover.
Sessions need a copy in the surviving region before the failure, with revocations following fast.

incidents.title: Both regions sold the last 300 consoles
incidents.brief: During a 4-minute transatlantic partition, GameVault's US and EU databases each promoted themselves and kept taking inventory writes at 9k req/s per region. 300 consoles were sold twice.
incidents.constraint: Inventory decrements cannot be merged afterwards; a brief write outage beats overselling.
incidents.question: What stops both sides accepting writes during a partition?

choices.label: Majority quorum with a third-region witness and fencing tokens
choices.resultBody: When the Atlantic link drops, US plus the witness hold 2 of 3 votes and keep writing; EU loses its lease and fencing tokens reject its stale writes. Oversells fall to 0, at the price of EU checkout failing during the 4-minute partition.

choices.label: Last-writer-wins on inventory rows by wall-clock timestamp
choices.resultBody: LWW keeps one of the two decrements and silently drops the other, so the stock count looks sane while 300 customers still hold orders for consoles that do not exist. 40 ms of clock skew also reorders writes.

choices.label: Cut heartbeat timeout to 2 s for faster self-promotion
choices.resultTitle: Split brain now triggers in 2 s
choices.resultBody: On an 80 ms link, routine packet loss now looks like a dead peer. Both sides self-promote three times a day instead of once a quarter, and oversold units climb to 520.

hints: Both regions believed they were the primary at the same time.
Two voters can never break a tie during a partition.
Leadership should require a majority vote, and an ex-leader's writes must be rejectable.

incidents.title: Standby region collapses under failover traffic
incidents.brief: PetPals keeps 4 pods warm in eu-central for 80 needed. On failover, autoscaling asked for 76 more during a regional event and got 9 in 25 minutes; error rate hit 85%.
incidents.constraint: The budget cannot pay for a full second copy of production.
incidents.question: How big must the standby be, and what covers the gap?

choices.label: Keep 50% capacity warm and shed low-priority traffic on failover

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Pays for 40 idle pods; recommendations and feeds degrade for ~20 min while autoscaling fills in.

choices.resultBody: Forty pre-provisioned pods, plus reserved capacity for the rest, take the load on day one. Load shedding drops recommendation and feed calls, about 45% of requests, so checkout and login stay under 1.5% errors while autoscaling adds the remaining pods. Cost: about $14k a month for capacity that sits idle.

choices.label: Rely on autoscaling from 4 to 80 pods at failover
choices.resultBody: During a regional outage every tenant fails over into the same zones, instance requests return insufficient-capacity errors, and new nodes take minutes to boot even when granted; the 4 pods melt long before help arrives.

choices.label: Speed up failover so traffic moves in 30 seconds
choices.resultBody: Full traffic now reaches 4 pods 30 seconds after the outage instead of 3 minutes, so they saturate sooner, crash-loop under load and slow the autoscaler's readiness checks even further.

hints: The standby was sized for idle time, not for the worst day.
Cloud capacity is least available exactly when a whole region fails.
Decide how much must be pre-provisioned and what you'll switch off until the rest arrives.

incidents.title: EU profiles indexed in a US cluster
incidents.brief: Legal found 2.1M EU user profiles indexed in LinkUp's only search cluster, in us-east. EU searches also pay the Atlantic round trip: p95 is 340 ms at 6k req/s.
incidents.constraint: EU personal data may not be stored outside the EU; the US cluster stays for US users.
incidents.question: Where should EU profiles be indexed and served from?

choices.label: EU-resident search cluster, routed by the user's home region
choices.resultBody: EU profiles are re-indexed in eu-central and deleted from us-east; EU search skips the ~90 ms Atlantic hop and p95 falls from 340 to 45 ms. Cost: a second cluster (~$6k/month), and global admin search must federate over non-PII fields.

choices.label: Encrypt EU documents in the US cluster with EU-held keys
choices.resultBody: Counsel rejects it: the 2.1M profiles still live in us-east, just encrypted. Encrypted fields also cannot be tokenized for full-text search, so relevance collapses and decrypt-on-read pushes p95 to 410 ms.

choices.label: Cache EU search responses at Frankfurt CDN edge nodes
choices.resultTitle: Faster, and now PII is in two places
choices.resultBody: About 40% of repeat queries hit the edge, so p95 dips to 210 ms, but the index is still in us-east and search results containing personal data are now cached at edge PoPs too.

hints: This is a legal constraint first and a latency problem second.
Encrypting or caching data does not change where it is stored.
Partition the data by where each user legally belongs, and route requests the same way.

incidents.title: Every customer invoiced twice on the 1st
incidents.brief: After going active-active, InvoiceIQ's monthly billing cron runs in both us-east and eu-west. Each region billed all 48k customers at 00:00 UTC, and 96k invoice emails went out in 20 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Billing must still run on the 1st even if one region is down.
incidents.question: How do two live regions split a job that must run once?

choices.label: Each region bills only customers homed there; survivors adopt orphans

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Ownership is data, not timing; takeover of a dead region's customers is a deliberate step.

choices.resultBody: Every customer row has a home_region, and each cron only bills its own. Because each customer is written by one region, the invoice row's unique key also works. If a region is marked failed, the survivor adopts its customers after the failover is declared, so billing still runs. Cost: takeover is an explicit, audited step.

choices.label: Add a unique index on (customer, period) in each regional DB
choices.resultBody: Each region's insert succeeds against its own copy before replication delivers the other one about 400 ms later; the conflict is detected after both crons already emailed the invoice.

choices.label: Disable the billing cron in eu-west permanently
choices.resultBody: Duplicates stop, but billing lives in one region again: when us-east is down on the 1st, nobody bills, and the next outage delays 48k invoices by 30 hours until someone runs it by hand.

hints: Both regions are healthy and both believe the job is theirs.
With async replication, 'check the database first' sees only your own region's writes.
Give each unit of work exactly one owner, and make handing it over explicit.

incidents.title: Listing photos 404 after failing over to eu-west
incidents.brief: RentNest serves 90 TB of listing photos from a us-east bucket. During the failover drill to eu-west, the app ran fine but 38% of photos broke: the CDN had only the hot ones cached.
incidents.constraint: New uploads must be viewable by the host within 5 seconds.
incidents.question: How do photos stay available when their home region is gone?

choices.label: Replicate the bucket cross-region; read local, fall back on 404

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Doubles storage and pays replication transfer; brand-new uploads may lag seconds.

choices.resultTitle: The photos were already in Europe
choices.resultBody: Every object is copied to an eu-west bucket, most within seconds. The CDN and app read the nearest copy and fall back to the other bucket on a 404, which covers a brand-new upload that hasn't replicated yet. During the drill only uploads from the last few seconds went missing. Cost: double storage plus replication transfer.

choices.label: Raise the CDN cache TTL on photos to 30 days
choices.resultTitle: The long tail was never cached
choices.resultBody: Popular photos stay cached longer, but most of the 90 TB is rarely viewed and never in the cache, so 21% of requests still miss to a dead origin, and new uploads can't be written anywhere.

choices.label: Have the app write every upload to both regions' buckets
choices.resultTitle: Copies drift with nothing to repair them
choices.resultBody: Uploads now wait on a cross-region PUT, adding 120 ms, and whenever one write fails the buckets silently diverge; the 90 TB already uploaded was never copied, so old listings remain broken.

hints: The app failed over; its data didn't.
A cache holds what was popular, not everything you own.
Object stores can copy data across regions for you, but the copy trails the original.

incidents.title: EU logins 401 after key rotation
incidents.brief: PayLink rotated its JWT signing key in the us-east vault only. After traffic failed over to eu-west, EU pods verified with the stale key and 4,200 logins/s returned 401.
incidents.constraint: Keys rotate every 30 days, and either region must be able to take 100% of traffic at any time.
incidents.question: How should the key rotation roll out across regions?

choices.label: Two-phase rotation: replicate new key everywhere, then sign
choices.resultBody: The new key reaches both vaults and the JWKS first; pods accept old and new keys for one 60-minute token lifetime, and only then does signing switch. 401s fall from 4,200/s to 0. Cost: each rotation takes an hour and needs a vault replication-lag alert.

choices.label: Point EU pods at the us-east vault over the WAN
choices.resultTitle: EU auth now depends on us-east
choices.resultBody: Verification works today, but every key-cache miss crosses an 85 ms WAN hop, p95 rises to 180 ms, and the next us-east outage takes EU logins down with it, which is the failover this incident was about.

choices.label: Rolling restart of EU pods after every key rotation
choices.resultTitle: Restart reloads the same stale key
choices.resultBody: Pods reload from the EU vault replica, which never received the new key, so they come back verifying with the old one. 401s stay near 3,900/s and the 20-minute rollout removes capacity mid-incident.

hints: The failover region was running, but it did not have everything it needed.
A new key must be trusted everywhere before anything signs with it.
Split rotation into distribute-and-accept, then switch-signing, with an overlap window.

incidents.title: First real failover finds hard-coded us-east hosts
incidents.brief: Norvo's DR plan promised 15-minute failover. In the first real us-east outage, eu-west took 3 h 40 min: 11 services had us-east hostnames in config and the runbook's 14 steps were stale.
incidents.constraint: Leadership wants proof failover works, not another document.
incidents.question: How do you know failover will work before you need it?

choices.label: Evacuate a production region every quarter during game days

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Planned, staffed risk each quarter in exchange for known recovery time.

choices.resultBody: Draining real traffic out of a region on a planned day surfaced the hard-coded hosts, a missing secret and two quotas; each became a fix and an automated check. The next outage fails over in 18 minutes because the path is exercised every quarter. Cost: a staffed, scheduled risk and some engineering time each drill.

choices.label: Rewrite the DR runbook with detailed step-by-step screenshots
choices.resultBody: The runbook is correct on the day it's written, but services keep adding new dependencies; without exercising the path, the next outage still finds four new us-east hostnames and takes 2.5 hours.

choices.label: Replicate every database to eu-west synchronously
choices.resultBody: Every write now pays an 80 ms cross-region round trip, yet in the next outage the eu-west services still call us-east hostnames and wait on the same broken config.

hints: The data had replicated fine; the services around it hadn't been tested.
Anything that isn't exercised regularly drifts.
Treat failover as a routine operation you practise with real traffic.

incidents.title: Column drop in us-east breaks eu-west mid-deploy
incidents.brief: Fitbase deploys region by region. v42 renamed users.phone to phone_e164 in one migration; replication applied the DDL in eu-west while v41 still ran there, and 30% of eu-west requests failed.
incidents.constraint: Regions must keep deploying one at a time, hours apart.
incidents.question: How do you change a shared schema while regions run different versions?

choices.label: Add and dual-write the new column; drop the old one last

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Four releases instead of one; both columns exist for weeks.

choices.resultTitle: Old and new code both find their column
choices.resultBody: Release 1 adds phone_e164 and dual-writes; a backfill copies old rows; release 2 reads the new column; only after every region runs it does release 3 drop phone. At no point does a running version lose a column it reads. Cost: four releases over a few weeks instead of one.

choices.label: Deploy v42 to all regions at the same moment
choices.resultBody: A rolling deploy still has old and new pods side by side for minutes in every region, so old pods keep failing on the missing column, and a bad release now hits all regions at once with no staged rollback.

choices.label: Pause replication to eu-west until its deploy finishes
choices.resultTitle: Four hours of lag builds up
choices.resultBody: eu-west errors pause, but its data falls four hours behind, users see stale profiles, and if us-east fails meanwhile you lose four hours of writes; when replication resumes the DDL breaks v41 anyway.

hints: During a region-by-region rollout, two versions share one schema for hours.
A migration is safe only if both the old and the new code can run against it.
Split the rename into steps that each stay backward-compatible.

incidents.title: Two users claim the same @handle in different regions
incidents.brief: Chirply runs DynamoDB global tables in us and eu. Handle signup checks a GSI, then writes. Replication takes about 1 s, so 140 handles a day end up owned by two accounts.
incidents.constraint: Normal posting and reads must stay local and fast in each region.
incidents.question: How do you enforce a globally unique handle?

choices.label: Keep just the handles table in a cross-region quorum store

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Handle claims pay one cross-region round trip; everything else stays local.

choices.resultTitle: Only the rare write pays the latency
choices.resultBody: Handle claims go through a store that commits only with a majority across regions, so the second claimant's conditional insert fails. This is the PACELC trade in miniature: 300 claims/s pay about 90 ms extra, while millions of posts stay local and eventually consistent. Cost: one more datastore to run.

choices.label: Check both regions' indexes for the handle before writing
choices.resultBody: Two users who claim within the same second both check both regions, both find the handle free, and both write; the race narrows but check-then-write across async replicas can't close it.

choices.label: Switch the GSI lookup to a strongly consistent read
choices.resultBody: DynamoDB global secondary indexes only support eventually consistent reads, and even a strong base-table read is strong only within one region; the other region's pending write is still invisible.

hints: Each region confirmed 'free' using only what had replicated to it.
Uniqueness is a global decision; async replicas can only tell you about the past.
Pay for coordination only on the small path that truly needs it.

incidents.title: Carts drop items after a region hop
incidents.brief: CartNest runs active-active in us-east and ap-south. When a phone and a laptop edit one cart through different regions, 3.2% of carts silently lose items at 24k req/s.
incidents.constraint: Both regions must keep accepting cart writes locally; a 150 ms cross-region write is not allowed.
incidents.question: How should concurrent cart edits from two regions merge?

choices.label: Merge carts as an add-wins OR-Set CRDT per item
choices.resultBody: Adds from both regions merge per item instead of one whole cart overwriting the other, so lost items fall from 3.2% of carts to 0. Cost: tombstones grow cart documents ~18% until compaction, and a remove racing an add keeps the item.

choices.label: Tighten NTP to 1 ms so last-writer-wins orders edits
choices.resultBody: Clocks now agree within 1 ms, but the phone and laptop edits are truly concurrent. LWW still keeps one whole cart and discards the other, so 3.1% of carts keep losing items.

choices.label: Pin every cart's writes to one home region
choices.resultBody: A single writer per cart ends conflicts, but ap-south shoppers homed in us-east now write across a 150 ms round trip; cart p95 rises from 60 to 210 ms, breaking the stated constraint.

hints: The edits are not wrong; they are concurrent.
Picking one winner by time always throws the other edit away.
Use a data type whose merge is commutative, so both regions converge on the union.
